paragraphs.text: Autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia-51 is a complex neurologic disorder that begins in infancy. Hypotonia progresses to spastic paraplegia or tetraplegia, and patients have microcephaly, severe to profound intellectual disability, absent or very limited speech, inability to walk, stereotypic laughter, drooling, and growth retardation. Some patients have seizures (Moreno-De-Luca et al., 2011; Abou Jamra et al., 2011; Kong et al., 2013). The disorder belongs to a group of clinically similar conditions, called 'AP-4 deficiency syndrome', that are caused by mutations in genes encoding subunits of the adaptor protein complex-4 (AP-4) (Moreno-De-Luca et al., 2011; Kong et al., 2013).

paragraphs.text: Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) described a brother and sister from a consanguineous Palestinian-Jordanian family with an autosomal recessive form of spastic tetraplegic cerebral palsy. Both sibs also had profound intellectual disability, microcephaly, epilepsy, stereotypic laughter, drooling, and similar facial dysmorphism. Neither sib developed normal speech or sphincter control, and both became wheelchair-bound.

paragraphs.text: The female sib (IV-4) in the family reported by Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) was born at term and had microcephaly and hypotonia at birth. By the first year of life this had progressed to spastic tetraplegia with hyperreflexia and generalized hypertonia. She never spoke or walked independently. She had been wheelchair-bound since age 5 years, when generalized tonic-clonic seizures began. At age 23 she had microcephaly (-3 SD), profound cognitive impairment, drooling, stereotypic laughter, and facial dysmorphism. Brain MRI showed ventriculomegaly, cortical and cerebellar atrophy, reduced hippocampal volume, and diffuse white matter loss that was most pronounced frontally and in the corpus callosum. EEG showed generalized theta slowing.

paragraphs.text: Her brother (IV-5) was also born at term and had microcephaly and hypotonia after birth, with developmental delay evident by the first year of life (Moreno-De-Luca et al., 2011). He acquired only some dysarthric words and could walk with support, but increasing spasticity made him wheelchair-dependent by age 9 years. His seizures began as staring spells and became generalized tonic-clonic seizures at age 15. At age 22 he had spastic tetraplegia with hypertonia and hyperreflexia, stereotypic laughter, drooling, jerky nystagmus, and severe cognitive deficits. Head CT showed moderate ventriculomegaly with slightly prominent cisterns.

paragraphs.text: Abou Jamra et al. (2011) reported 8 affected individuals from 3 consanguineous families. They had severe intellectual disability, absent speech, a shy character, stereotypic laughter, muscular hypotonia that progressed to spastic paraplegia, microcephaly, foot deformity, decreased muscle mass of the lower limbs, inability to walk, and growth retardation. One of these families carried an AP4E1 mutation (see MOLECULAR GENETICS).

paragraphs.text: Kong et al. (2013) reported 3-year-old identical twin girls born to first-cousin Moroccan parents. The twins had complex hereditary spastic paraplegia with onset in infancy. Features included marked developmental delay, microcephaly (head circumference -2 SD and -2.5 SD), severe intellectual disability, inability to walk, absent speech, early infantile hypotonia, and spastic paraplegia of the lower limbs. They also had stereotypic laughter, drooling and other pseudobulbar signs, short stature, and low body weight. Their facial gestalt included a prominent bulbous nose, a wide mouth, and coarse features. CT showed atrophy of the inferior vermis with cortical atrophy, and EEG showed diffuse slow waves. The twins had no seizures, hyperreflexia, or Babinski signs. Kong et al. (2018) later reported the same twins at age 8 years and noted that their pregnancy had no complications, but that neonatal asphyxia was noted at delivery.

paragraphs.text: Both twins reported by Kong et al. (2013) had received BCG vaccination a few days after birth. At 9 months of age each developed a unilateral enlarged, inflamed axillary lymph node. Biopsy of the surgically removed nodes showed acid-fast bacilli consistent with mycobacterial infection. Neither twin had another mycobacterial episode by age 3 years. Kong et al. (2013) proposed that the AP4E1 mutation was the most likely cause of the mycobacterial disease (see GENOTYPE/PHENOTYPE CORRELATIONS). However, Kong et al. (2018) later attributed the Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (MSMD) in these twins to a homozygous SPPL2A splice mutation (c.733+1G-A). They stated that the twins' hereditary spastic paraplegia was due to the homozygous AP4E1 mutation.

paragraphs.text: Kong et al. (2013) found no immunologic abnormality to explain the mycobacterial disease in the twins with SPG51. Leukocyte subsets, immunoglobulins, and complement were normal. The IL-12/IFN-gamma circuit, IFN-gamma-induced GAF DNA binding, and superoxide production were also normal. Exome data showed no causative mutation in known MSMD genes. A heterozygous IFNGR1 Q190R variant and an IL12RB2 K768N variant were judged nonfunctional.

paragraphs.text: In 2 consanguineous families with the same phenotype as their AP4E1 family, Abou Jamra et al. paragraphs.text: Kong et al. (2013) identified a homozygous arg1105-to-ter (R1105X) mutation in the AP4E1 gene in identical twin girls, born to first-cousin Moroccan parents, who had complex hereditary spastic paraplegia with onset in infancy. The mutation was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The parents were heterozygous and a healthy sib was wildtype. The mutation was absent from 1,050 CEPH controls from 51 ethnic groups and from 69 Moroccan controls. It did not alter AP4E1 mRNA levels or splicing in patient cells, but AP-4-epsilon protein was barely detectable. Assembled AP-4 complex was reduced by more than 95% in patient fibroblasts and EBV-B cells, and the AP-4 binding partner tepsin was lost. The twins also had BCG-related mycobacterial lymphadenitis, which Kong et al. (2013) suggested might result from a dominant-negative or gain-of-function effect of the truncated protein. Kong et al. (2018) later attributed the mycobacterial disease to a coexisting homozygous SPPL2A splice mutation and stated that the spastic paraplegia was due to the homozygous AP4E1 R1105X mutation.
